Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-XXVII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. source_text: THESIS I. THESIBUS ante editis ostendimus Scholae Romanae Doctores cum Protestantibus in eo, verbis saltem, consentire, quod in statu Naturae Lapsae liberum hominis Arbitrium, sine Gratia Christi nihil omnino possit, in iis quae ad veram pietatem pertinent, & per se aeternae saluti conducunt: & tamen, quum Liberum hominis lapsi Arbitrium consideratur respectu boni salutaris & spiritualis, Doctores Scholae Romanae non eodem modo de illo cum Protestantibus loquuntur.
english: Our earlier theses established a verbal agreement, at any rate, between Rome's doctors and the Protestants: once nature has fallen, a man's free choice achieves nothing whatever apart from Christ's grace where true piety and the things that of themselves lead to eternal salvation are concerned.
But when they turn to fallen man's free choice as it stands toward saving, spiritual good, Rome's doctors and the Protestants use different language.

source_text: II. Primo enim Scholae Romanae Theologi, quantumlibet gratiae divinae auxilium ad pietatis opera necessarium agnoscant, nihilominus dici volunt hominem in rebus divinis & spiritualibus, etiam ante gratiam, esse Liberi arbitrii. Non quod in eo genere sine gratia quicquam possit, sed quia, mediante auxilio gratiae, libere potest bonum spirituale amplecti, & sic ut veram potestatem habeat illud rejiciendi, atque ab eo recedendi.
english: First, the theologians of the Roman School, however much they acknowledge that the help of divine grace is necessary for works of piety, still want it said that man has free choice in divine and spiritual things even before grace.

They do not mean that he can do anything of that kind without grace, but that, with the help of grace, he can freely embrace spiritual good, and in such a way that he has a real power to reject it and turn away from it.

source_text: III. Hanc doctrinam ut toti Scholae Romanae communem proponit & refert Bellarminus libro sexto de Libero Arbitrio pluribus in locis. Praesertim vero capite decimo quinto, ubi haec est prima illius sententia. Homo ante omnem gratiam, liberum habet arbitrium, non solum ad opera naturalia & moralia, sed etiam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia. Quo sensu autem istud ab eo asseratur, patet ex ejusdem libri capite nono. Ubi quaestionem his verbis proponit, Sitne homo, post lapsum primi hominis, vere liberi arbitrii in iis rebus quae pertinent ad salutem, ut quamvis nihil possit sine auxilio Gratiae, tamen per gratiam praevenientem excitatus & a Deo adjutus, ita valeat operari, ut possit etiam non operari.
english: Bellarmine sets this out, as the shared view of the entire Roman School, at many points in the sixth book of his treatise on free choice, above all in chapter 15. His first proposition there is: 'Prior to any grace, man possesses free choice not merely for natural and moral works but for works of piety and supernatural works too.'

What he means by this emerges from chapter 9 of that book, where the question is framed as follows: 'Since the first man's fall, does man really have free choice in matters of salvation? That is, granted he can do nothing without grace's help, once prevenient grace has stirred him and God assists him, can he act in such a way that he is also able not to act?'

source_text: IV. Atque huc spectat Canon Concilii Tridentini qui est quartus Sessionis sextae. Si quis dixerit, Liberum hominis Arbitrium a Deo motum & excitatum nihil cooperari assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocanti, quo ad obtinendam justificationis gratiam se disponat, ac praeparet, neque posse dissentire, si velit, sed velut inanime quoddam nihil omnino agere, mereque passive se habere: anathema sit.
english: Trent's sixth session, in its fourth canon, has the same aim. It runs: 'If anyone says that man's free choice, moved and roused by God, cooperates not at all by assenting to God who rouses and calls, whereby it disposes and prepares itself to obtain the grace of justification; that it cannot dissent if it wishes; but that like some lifeless thing it does nothing whatever and is merely passive: let him be anathema.'

source_text: V. Porro Scholae Romanae Doctores circa modum quo gratia divina efficax est, multum inter se dissentiunt: dum alii volunt gratiam libero arbitrio non solum novas vires tribuere, hominemque ad bene agendum invitare & sollicitare, aut etiam in bene agendo adjuvare quod omnes concedunt; sed etiam tantam ejus esse efficaciam, ut voluntatem ad bene agendum flectat & determinet infallibiliter & insuperabiliter: alii vero istud negant, ut pluribus alias a nobis ostensum est. Caeterum omnes in eo conveniunt, quantacunque sit gratiae divinae efficacia, illam nihilominus a libero arbitrio non tollere potestatem repudiandi bonum ad quod hominem movet atque allicit. Adeoque illi ipsi qui pertendunt gratiam per se efficacem esse, & conversionis actum infallibiliter in homine operari, conformiter tamen Canoni Tridentino fatentur semper in homine manere potestatem a gratia dissentiendi, & illi resistendi. Ac proinde omnes in eo consentiunt liberum arbitrium per gratiam praeventum & excitatum, sic posse bene operari, ut contrarium in ejus facultate maneat.
english: The doctors of the Roman School differ widely among themselves on how divine grace is efficacious. Some hold that grace not only gives free choice new strength, invites and urges man to do good, or even helps him in doing it, which all grant, but also that its efficacy is so great that it bends and determines the will to do good infallibly and irresistibly. Others deny this, as we have shown more fully elsewhere.
But all agree that, however great the efficacy of divine grace, it still does not take from free choice the power to reject the good to which it moves and draws a man.

So even those who maintain that grace is efficacious of itself and works the act of conversion in man infallibly still admit, in line with the canon of Trent, that man always keeps the power to dissent from grace and resist it. Thus all agree that free choice, once grace has gone before it and roused it, can do good in such a way that the contrary remains within its power.

source_text: VI. Itaque pertendunt Liberum arbitrium, respectu boni ipsius salutaris, per peccatum extinctum & amissum non esse, sed solum debilitatum, fauciatum & attenuatum. Qua in re sequuntur doctrinam Synodi Tridentinae, cujus hic quoque Canon est quintus Sessionis sextae. Si quis liberum hominis arbitrium post Adae peccatum amissum & extinctum esse dixerit, aut rem esse de solo titulo, imo titulum sine re, figmentum denique a Satana invectum in Ecclesiam: anathema sit.
english: So they maintain that free choice, even with respect to saving good, was not extinguished and lost through sin, but only weakened, wounded and diminished. Here they follow the teaching of the Synod of Trent, whose canon on this point is the fifth of the sixth session:

'If anyone says that man's free choice was lost and extinguished after Adam's sin, or that it is a thing in name only, indeed a name without a reality, in short a fiction brought into the Church by Satan: let him be anathema.'

source_text: VII. Liberum autem arbitrium, etiam in spiritualibus, non penitus amissum & extinctum esse volunt, sed duntaxat fauciatum atque attenuatum, quia post peccatum in homine mansit, & ante gratiam superest, potentia quaedam remota & imperfecta ad opera pietatis facienda: licet ad eadem opera potentiam perfectam & proximam non habeat, & nihil omnino ex se hac in parte facere valeat. Istud videre est apud Bellarminum libro quinto de libero arbitrio capite decimo quinto, ubi haec est ejus secunda sententia. Habet homo ante omnem gratiam potentiam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis facienda. Tertia vero sententia haec est. Non habet homo ante omnem gratiam potentiam proximam & perfectam ad opera pietatis: & ideo nihil omnino in hoc genere ex se facere potest.
english: Their reason for calling free choice wounded and weakened rather than wholly lost and extinguished, even in spiritual matters, is this: after sin, and still prior to grace, there survives in man some remote, imperfect capacity for works of piety. What he lacks for such works is a complete, proximate capacity; so on that side he can accomplish nothing whatever by himself.

See Bellarmine on free choice, book 5, chapter 15. Proposition two there reads: 'Prior to any grace, man has a remote, imperfect capacity for doing works of piety.' Proposition three reads: 'Prior to any grace, man lacks a proximate, complete capacity for works of piety; hence by himself he can do absolutely nothing of that kind.'

source_text: VIII. Porro haec verba Bellarmini, quibus asserit in iis quae salutem & pietatem spectant, hominem nihil omnino ex se facere posse, explicant quo sensu tribuat homini peccatori & gratia Dei destituto potentiam quandam imperfectam ad spirituale & salutare bonum. Nec enim propterea existimat hominem sine gratia in eo genere aliquid praestare quidem posse, verum languide atque imperfecte: sed solum mens ejus est, in homine manere post peccatum potentiam quandam, quae viribus novis per gratiam acceptis, in bonum spirituale libere ferri potest, circa quod ante per se sola nihil omnino agere poterat. Quod observat ipse Bellarminus respondens ad hoc Kemnitii dilemma. Aut habet homo ex se aliquas vires, quamvis exiles; aut nullas omnino. Si habet aliquas, ergo potest aliquid sine Dei gratia. Si nullas; ergo extinctum est liberum arbitrium. Respondet enim hominem habere potentiam tantum remotam & vires imperfectas, & ideo nihil per se posse. Sed si perficiatur ea potentia, & vires addantur, illum posse multa praestare.
english: These words of Bellarmine, in which he says that man can do nothing at all of himself in what concerns salvation and piety, show in what sense he ascribes to the sinner who lacks God's grace an imperfect power for spiritual and saving good.

He does not think that without grace a man can achieve something of that kind, if only feebly and imperfectly. He means only that after sin there remains in man a certain power which, once it receives new strength through grace, can move freely toward spiritual good, though before, left to itself, it could do nothing at all about it.

Bellarmine himself makes this point in answering Chemnitz's dilemma: 'Either man has some strength of his own, however slight, or none at all. If he has some, then he can do something without God's grace; if none, then free choice is extinguished.' He replies that man has only a remote power and imperfect strength, and so can do nothing by himself; but if that power is perfected and strength is added, he can achieve a great deal.

source_text: IX. Ut ostendat autem quomodo homo ante gratiam arbitrium liberum habeat, etiam in spiritualibus, cum tamen ante gratiam bonum facere non possit; dicit in eo statu arbitrium hominis liberum quidem eo respectu esse: sed tamen ejus libertatem esse quasi ligatam atque impeditam: solvi autem & expediri, quum potentia proxima ad operandum per Dei gratiam praevenientem ei confertur. Atque ut eam rem illustret, Simile, inquit, aliquid experimur in potentia videndi: nam absente specie sensibili, habet homo potentiam & libertatem videndi: non enim ea species causa est libertatis, aut potentiae videndi; sed tamen potentia remota est, & libertas ligata, donec accepta specie potentia perficiatur, & in actum prodire possit.
english: To show how man before grace has free choice even in spiritual things, though before grace he cannot do good, he says that in that state man's choice is indeed free in that respect, but its freedom is, as it were, bound and hindered. It is untied and released when the proximate power to act is given to it by God's prevenient grace.

He illustrates this: 'We find something like it in the power of sight. When the sensible image is absent, a man has the power and freedom to see, for that image is not the cause of the freedom or of the power of seeing. Yet the power is remote and the freedom bound until the image is received, the power is completed, and it can go out into act.'

source_text: X. Praeterea vero notandum est, quum Bellarminus dicit libertatem hominis circa bonum spirituale per peccatum fuisse ligatam, non extinctam, mentem ejus non esse, quod liberum arbitrium per gratiam solutum, & bono consentiens, atque illud prosequens, id faciat per vires quas jam ante habebat, non quas gratia de novo ipsi suppeditavit: sicut homo cujus soluta sunt vincula, dum ambulat id facit per vires quas jam ante habebat, & quae de novo ipsi non sunt additae, sed solum quarum usus impedimento quodam cohibebatur. Queritur enim Kemnitium per fraudem & deceptionem simile quid Catholicis Doctoribus imputare. Scribit Kemnitius, inquit, Catholicos in ea sententia esse, ut liberum arbitrium per gratiam excitatum exerat vires quas habebat, etiam antequam excitaretur, & per illas suas vires vocationi divinae consentiat: ita ut gratia praeveniens non tribuat vires libero arbitrio, sed quasi sopitas excitet. At non hoc sentiunt Catholici: sed agnoscunt quidem liberum arbitrium in homine, etiam antequam eum gratia divina praeveniat: quia liberum arbitrium est res naturalis, quae per peccatum non amittitur: sed tamen non dicunt, nec sentiunt liberum arbitrium habere potentiam ullam, saltem proximam, ad actus pietatis, sed eam accipere a Deo per gratiam praevenientem. Cap. 13. Responsione ad primum argumentum.
english: It should also be noted that when Bellarmine says man's freedom regarding spiritual good was bound by sin, not extinguished, he does not mean that free choice, set loose by grace and consenting to good and pursuing it, does so by strength it already had and not by strength newly supplied by grace. That would be like a man whose chains are taken off: when he walks, he does so by strength he already had, which was not newly added to him, only its use held back by some hindrance.

In fact he complains that Chemnitz fraudulently and deceptively attributes something like this to the Catholic doctors. 'Chemnitz writes,' he says, 'that the Catholics hold that free choice, roused by grace, puts forth the strength it had even before it was roused, and by that strength of its own consents to God's call, so that prevenient grace does not give strength to free choice but only wakes it, as it were, from sleep.

The Catholics do not think this. They do acknowledge free choice in man even before divine grace goes before him, since free choice is a natural thing and is not lost through sin. But they do not say or think that free choice has any power, at least any proximate power, for acts of piety; it receives that from God through prevenient grace.' Chapter 13, answer to the first argument.

source_text: XI. Itaque Bellarminus eodem loco docet liberum arbitrium hominis peccatoris ex se non habere ut cooperetur ad ipsius conversionem, sed cooperandi potestatem a gratia recipere. Sicut lapis, inquit, ex se non habet, ut cooperetur, si forte convertatur in carnem; sic etiam liberum arbitrium ex se non habet, ut cooperetur ad suam ipsius conversionem: potest tamen a Deo recipere potestatem operandi per gratiam praevenientem, quod non potest lapis.
english: So Bellarmine teaches in the same place that a sinner's free choice does not have from itself the ability to cooperate in its own conversion, but receives the power to cooperate from grace.

'Just as a stone,' he says, 'does not have from itself the ability to cooperate if it should happen to be turned into flesh, so free choice does not have from itself the ability to cooperate in its own conversion. Yet it can receive from God, through prevenient grace, the power to act, which a stone cannot.'

source_text: XII. Quae doctrina est ipsius Ludovici Molinae. Docet enim consensum quem voluntas nostra praebet Deo per gratiam praevenientem vocanti, a Deo esse non tantum tanquam ab alliciente, invitante, & excitante, sed etiam tanquam a cooperante per auxilium gratiae; adeoque in eo consensu nihil reipsa esse quod supernaturale non sit; ac proinde adultum nihil habere, in iis quae ad justificationem necessaria sunt, de quo gloriari possit, & quod a Deo per gratiam non acceperit. Sic enim ex antepositis quibusdam ratiocinatur. Quo fit ut consensus liberi arbitrii Deo excitanti ac vocanti per gratiam praevenientem, nihil in re sit quod non sit supernaturale, & quod non simul a Deo emanet, non solum tanquam ab alliciente, excitante, & invitante ad id arbitrium nostrum, sed etiam tanquam a cooperante per auxilium gratiae, atque adeo fit ut nihil omnino habeat adultus ex iis, quae ad justificationem sunt necessaria, & quibus a non justificato discernatur, de quo gloriari possit, ac si id a Deo non acceperit; tametsi ad multa ex iis, quae ad justificationem sunt necessaria, libere cooperetur ac influat; ita ut in ipsius potestate sit non cooperari, & non influere, atque adeo impedire ne in rerum natura existant. Disputatione 40. ad art. 3. quaest. 14.
english: This is the teaching of Luis de Molina himself. He holds that the consent our will gives to God calling it through prevenient grace comes from God not only as one who attracts, invites and rouses, but also as one who cooperates through the help of grace. So there is nothing in that consent that is not in fact supernatural, and in what is needed for justification the adult has nothing to boast of that he has not received from God through grace.

He reasons this way from earlier premises: 'Hence in the consent of free choice to God, who rouses and calls through prevenient grace, there is in fact nothing that is not supernatural and does not also come from God, not only as attracting, rousing and inviting our choice to it, but also as cooperating through the help of grace.

So the adult has nothing at all, among the things needed for justification and by which he is set apart from the unjustified, that he can boast of as though he had not received it from God; even though in many of the things needed for justification he freely cooperates and contributes, so that it is in his power not to cooperate or contribute, and so to prevent them from coming into existence.' Disputation 40, on article 3 of question 14.

source_text: XIII. Ideoque statim anathema dicit illis qui affirmaverint consensum quem praebemus Deo excitanti per gratiam praevenientem, naturalem esse, aut posse elici sine ejusdem praevenientis gratiae auxilio & cooperatione. Nostra itaque sententia, inquit, anathema censeri debet, qui affirmaverit consensum arbitrii nostri Deo excitanti & vocanti per auxilium gratiae praevenientis, esse actum naturalem, aut posse elici sine auxilio & cooperatione ejusdem praevenientis gratiae: sed iterum esse etiam anathema, qui dixerit eundem consensum non esse in libera arbitrii nostri, ad modum explicatum, potestate, cooperationemque liberam arbitrii nostri non esse necessariam ad supernaturales actus quibus ad gratiam disponimur, & quibus ab iis discernimur qui non justificantur.
english: So he at once pronounces anathema on those who affirm that the consent we give to God rousing us through prevenient grace is natural, or can be produced without the help and cooperation of that prevenient grace.

'In our judgement,' he says, 'anyone who affirms that the consent of our choice to God rousing and calling us through the help of prevenient grace is a natural act, or can be produced without the help and cooperation of that prevenient grace, must be held anathema. But anyone is also anathema who says that this consent is not within the free power of our choice, in the way explained, and that the free cooperation of our choice is not necessary for the supernatural acts by which we are disposed to grace and set apart from those who are not justified.'

source_text: XIV. Quanquam vero Scholae Romanae Doctores cum Concilio Tridentino statuant liberum hominis arbitrium cooperari Deo vocanti atque excitanti, & humanam voluntatem non solum active, sed libere se habere, respectu primorum actuum quibus ad Deum convertimur; ita ut allicienti & trahenti gratiae non solum consentire, sed & ab ea dissentire possit: fatentur tamen initium justificationis & conversionis nostrae a solo Deo esse, non a libero nostro arbitrio, & eo respectu hominem mere passive se habere. Id videre est apud Josephum Angles Episcopum Bosanensem, cujus haec est Conclusio, Initium nostrae justificationis non est a libero arbitrio nostro; sed est solum ab ipso Deo, nobis mere passive nos habentibus. Quod postea multis scripturae locis probat. Ut illo, Non vos me elegistis. Item, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et, Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. In floribus quaestionum Theologicarum, Tractatu de Libero Arbitrio, quaestione unica. Articulo 3. Difficultate 7. Conclusione 1.
english: The doctors of the Roman School, with the Council of Trent, hold that man's free choice cooperates with God as he calls and rouses it, and that the human will acts not only actively but freely in the first acts by which we turn to God, so that it can not only consent to grace that attracts and draws it but also dissent from it.

All the same, they concede that our justification and conversion start from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive. This can be seen in Joseph Angles, Bishop of Bosa, whose conclusion reads: 'The beginning of our justification lies not in our free choice. It lies solely in God himself, while we are merely passive.'

He goes on to support it with a number of scriptural texts: 'You did not choose me'; 'Apart from me you can do nothing'; 'No one can come to me unless my Father draws him.' (Flores theologicarum quaestionum, on free choice, the single question, article 3, difficulty 7, conclusion 1.)

source_text: XV. Atque ut eam rem illustret, in eodem articulo distinguit tria genera operum, quae ad nostram justificationem spectant. Nam dicit quaedam opera antecedere nostram justificationem, quaedam esse extrema, & quaedam intermedia. Primi generis sunt juxta ipsum, ipsa praedestinatio, vocatio interior per inspirationem & exterior per concionatorem, vocatio per flagella, terror poenarum, gloriae desiderium, &c. Secundi generis sunt infusiones qualitatum supernaturalium, ut infusio fidei & gratiae gratum facientis, sive justificantis. Tertii vero generis sunt opera intermedia, quae sequuntur post auxilia praevenientia, & antecedunt gratiam justificantem: quales sunt actus fidei, spei, dilectionis, & poenitentiae disponentes nos ad gratiam.
english: To illustrate the point, in the same article he distinguishes three kinds of works bearing on our justification. Some works, he says, go before our justification, some are final, and some lie between.

To the first kind belong, on his account, predestination itself, the inward call through inspiration and the outward call through the preacher, the call through scourges, the fear of punishment, the desire for glory, and so on. To the second belong the infusions of supernatural qualities, such as the infusion of faith and of the grace that makes us pleasing to God, that is, justifying grace.
To the third belong the intermediate works, which follow the prevenient helps and come before justifying grace: acts of faith, hope, love and penitence that dispose us to grace.

source_text: XVI. Haec vero tria operum genera docet inter se differre respectu causae efficientis, in hoc quod opera primi & secundi generis, ut auxilia praevenientia & gratia habitualis, sunt a Deo sine nobis; quemadmodum Petrus & Paulus passive tantum se habebant, & nihil cooperabantur, quando sunt a Christo vocati; & etiam quemadmodum aer passive se habet recipiens lumen a sole: qua ratione nobis, nihil in eo agentibus, induuntur virtutes infusae, quae sunt qualitates supernaturales: sed quod attinet opera tertii generis, quae sunt dispositiones intermediae ad gratiam, ad ea homo justificandus non se habet passive tantum, verum etiam active: quia hoc respectu Deo libere cooperatur, dum voluntas elicit actum poenitentiae, & amoris, & intellectus fidei actum producit. Septima difficultate ad art. 7.
english: He teaches that these three kinds of works differ with respect to their efficient cause. Works of the first and second kind, such as the prevenient helps and habitual grace, are from God without us. So Peter and Paul were merely passive and contributed nothing when Christ called them, and so the air is passive when it receives light from the sun; in this way the infused virtues, which are supernatural qualities, are put on us while we do nothing.

But as for works of the third kind, the intermediate dispositions to grace, the man who is to be justified is not merely passive toward them but also active. In this respect he cooperates freely with God, as the will produces the act of penitence and of love, and the intellect produces the act of faith. Seventh difficulty, on article 7.

source_text: XVII. Caeterum Jansenius agnoscit quidem post peccatum in homine mansisse facultatem quae dicitur liberum arbitrium, & per quam recte aut perperam volumus & agimus, quaeque, ut jam ex se ad malum prona est, ita & per gratiam ad bonum flecti potest, illudque libere amplecti: sed tamen pertendit, secundum Augustinum, & rei veritatem, bono sensu dici posse libertatem arbitrii, respectu veri & salutaris boni, per peccatum in homine perditam & amissam esse. Non quod peccatum hominem spoliaverit ea libertate, quae voluntati essentialis est; & quae coactioni ac determinationi per naturam opponitur: sed quia prorsus per peccatum in homine periit libertas illa ad bonum quae opponitur servituti, donec per Christi salvatoris gratiam liberetur hominis voluntas. Nempe, ex ejus sententia, homo per peccatum sic est factus peccati servus, ut quicquid agat non amplius nisi peccare possit. Quoniam potest quidem a singulis peccatis abstinere; sed quum ab uno peccato abstinet, in aliud incidit, & peccatum peccato, non veris virtutis actibus commutat. Quippe cujus voluntas affectu pravo a Deo aversa, & bonum suum in creaturis quaerens, donec sursum per Dei gratiam attollatur, a vero fine semper & ubique aberrat, & ideo quicquid agat, peccato carere non potest, ut prolixe videre est apud authorem illum libro de gratia primi hominis cap. 6. & 7. & De statu naturae lapsae lib. 2. cap. item 6. & 7. & pluribus aliis in locis.
english: Jansenius does grant that after sin there remained in man the faculty called free choice, by which we will and act rightly or wrongly; which, just as it is now of itself inclined to evil, can also be bent to good by grace and embrace it freely.

Yet he maintains, following Augustine and the truth of the matter, that the freedom of choice with respect to true and saving good can rightly be said to have been destroyed and lost in man through sin. Sin has not stripped man of the freedom essential to the will, which is opposed to compulsion and to determination by nature. What perished entirely in man through sin is the freedom for good that is opposed to bondage, until man's will is set free by the grace of Christ the Saviour.

In his view, sin has made man such a slave of sin that whatever he does, he can no longer do anything but sin. He can indeed refrain from particular sins, but when he refrains from one he falls into another and trades sin for sin, not for true acts of virtue.

For his will, turned from God by a perverse affection and seeking its good in creatures, always and everywhere strays from the true end until God's grace lifts it up, and so whatever it does cannot be free of sin. This is set out at length by that author in his book on the grace of the first man, chapters 6 and 7, in On the State of Fallen Nature, book 2, likewise chapters 6 and 7, and in many other places.

source_text: XVIII. Quod spectat autem Protestantes, tam eos qui Theologi Confessionis Augustanae, quam qui singulariter Reformati dicuntur, communi consensu docent, hominem lapsum, ante Christi gratiam, viribus omnibus destitutum esse in iis quae pertinent ad opera pietatis, quae per se ad salutem prosunt & referuntur, & actus internos ac spirituales virtutum Christianarum & Theologicarum: nec satis esse putant, si dicamus liberum nostrum arbitrium hoc respectu languere, & debilitatum esse, fractum & attenuatum, sed volunt illud prorsus extinctum & amissum esse: adeoque hominem ante gratiam comparari debere, non homini aegro & captivo, sed homini mortuo: juxta scripturae morem, quae saepe inculcat homines ex se & sine gratia in peccatis mortuos esse. Unde non patiuntur dici hominem, ante gratiam liberum arbitrium habere ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia, sed volunt illum eatenus libertate sua spoliatum esse.
english: The Protestants, both the theologians of the Augsburg Confession and those specifically called Reformed, teach by common consent that fallen man, before the grace of Christ, lacks all strength in what pertains to works of piety, which of themselves serve and are directed to salvation, and to the inward and spiritual acts of the Christian and theological virtues.

They do not think it enough to say that our free choice in this respect is faint, weakened, broken and diminished; they hold that it is entirely extinguished and lost. So man before grace must be compared not to a sick man or a captive but to a dead man, after the manner of Scripture, which often insists that men of themselves and without grace are dead in sins.
Hence they will not allow it to be said that man before grace has free choice for works of piety and supernatural works; they hold that to that extent he has been stripped of his freedom.

source_text: XIX. Ista & similia passim repetunt & plurimum urgent, non tantum Scholae Reformatae Doctores, sed & jam dicti Theologi Confessionis Augustanae, praesertim in eo qui liber Concordiae apud ipsos dicitur. Credimus, inquiunt, quantum abest, ut corpus mortuum seipsum vivificare, atque sibi ipsi corporalem vitam restituere possit, tantum abesse ut homo, qui ratione peccati spiritualiter mortuus est, seipsum in vitam spiritualem revocandi ullam facultatem habeat. Et propterea damnant errores eos qui docent, Licet homo non renatus, ratione liberi arbitrii, ante sui regenerationem infirmior quidem sit, quam ut conversionis suae initium facere, atque propriis viribus sese ad Deum convertere, & legi Dei toto corde parere valeat: tamen si Spiritus Sanctus praedicatione verbi initium fecerit, suamque gratiam in verbo homini obtulerit, tum hominis voluntatem, propriis & naturalibus suis viribus quodammodo aliquid, licet id modiculum, infirmum & languidum admodum sit, conversionem adjuvare, atque cooperari, & seipsam ad gratiam applicare, praeparare, eam apprehendere, amplecti, & Evangelio credere posse. In Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Augustanae Confessionis. Articulo 2.
english: The doctors of the Reformed School repeat and press these and similar points everywhere, and so do the theologians of the Augsburg Confession already mentioned, especially in the book they call the Book of Concord.

'We believe,' they say, 'that just as a dead body cannot bring itself to life or restore bodily life to itself, so a man who is spiritually dead because of sin has no ability whatever to call himself back to spiritual life.'

So they condemn the errors of those who teach: 'Although unregenerate man, as to free choice, is before his regeneration too weak to begin his conversion, turn himself to God by his own strength and obey God's law with his whole heart, yet once the Holy Spirit has made a beginning by the preaching of the word and offered his grace to man in the word, man's will by its own natural strength can in some way contribute something, however small, weak and feeble, to help and cooperate in conversion, apply and prepare itself for grace, grasp it, embrace it and believe the Gospel.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2.

source_text: XX. Et in solida eorundem articulorum declaratione & repetitione, quae in eodem libro Concordiae inserta est, damnant dogma synergistarum. Qui fingunt hominem in rebus spiritualibus non prorsus ad bonum esse mortuum, sed tantum graviter vulneratum & semimortuum esse. Et quamvis liberum arbitrium infirmius sit, quam ut initium facere, & seipsum propriis viribus ad Deum convertere, & legi Dei toto corde obedire possit: tamen si Spiritus Sanctus initium faciat, & nos per Evangelium vocet, gratiam suam, remissionem peccatorum, & aeternam salutem nobis offerat, tunc liberum arbitrium propriis suis naturalibus viribus Deo occurrere, & aliquo modo (aliquid saltem, etsi parum & languide) ad conversionem suam conferre, eam adjuvare, cooperari, sese ad gratiam praeparare & applicare, eam apprehendere, amplecti, Evangelio credere, & quidem in continuatione & conservatione hujus operis, propriis suis viribus, una cum Spiritu Sancto cooperari posse. Art. 2. in rejectione errorum num. 4.
english: The Book of Concord also contains the Solid Declaration, a fuller restatement of those articles, and there they condemn the synergists' doctrine. The synergists picture man in spiritual matters as not altogether dead to good, merely badly hurt and half dead.

They grant that free choice is too feeble to start, to turn itself to God by its own strength, or to obey God's law wholeheartedly. But once the Holy Spirit starts the work, summoning us by the Gospel and holding out his grace, forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation, free choice (they say) can go out to meet God with its own natural powers.

On this view it can contribute something to its own conversion, at least a little and weakly. It can assist and cooperate, ready and apply itself to grace, lay hold of it, embrace it and believe the Gospel. And as the work is continued and kept up, it can work alongside the Holy Spirit with its own powers. (Article 2, rejected errors, no. 4.)

source_text: XXI. Adeoque iidem Confessionis Augustanae Doctores cum Reformatis docent, in hominis conversione voluntatem ejus pure passive se habere, id est, nihil agere, sed solum motum atque actionem Spiritus Sancti in se recipere, quod inter alios sensit ipse Lutherus. Ut loco jam citato agnoscunt iidem Doctores.
english: So the same doctors of the Augsburg Confession teach, with the Reformed, that in a man's conversion his will is purely passive: it does nothing but only receives into itself the motion and action of the Holy Spirit. Luther himself held this, among others, as the same doctors acknowledge in the place already cited.

source_text: XXII. Propterea tamen non negant Protestantes quum peccator omittit actus fidei, spei, & charitatis, aliarumque virtutum quae in Evangelio ipsi praecipiuntur, omissionem istam liberam esse, adeoque poena & supplicio dignam: idque, juxta Reformatos, quoniam homo, utut gratia destitutus, sciens tamen & volens actus a Deo praescriptos omittit: nec ulla vi externa, aut impedimento Physico prohibetur, quominus iis defungatur, sed solum prava voluntatis propriae dispositione, quae nativam ejus in agendo libertatem non tollit. Quibus addi potest, juxta Confessionis Augustanae Doctores, gratiam Dei ad bene agendum necessariam omnibus hominibus quodammodo praesto esse, & Deum paratum esse illam omnibus & singulis conferre, si fecerint quod in ipsis est.
english: The Protestants do not therefore deny that when a sinner fails to perform the acts of faith, hope and charity and the other virtues commanded him in the Gospel, the omission is free and so deserves penalty and punishment.

According to the Reformed, this is because man, though without grace, still knowingly and willingly leaves undone the acts God prescribes. No outside force or physical obstacle keeps him from performing them, only the perverse disposition of his own will, which does not remove his native freedom in acting.

To this may be added that, according to the doctors of the Augsburg Confession, the grace of God needed to do good is in some way available to all men, and God is ready to give it to each and every one if they do what lies in them.

source_text: XXIII. Praeterea quanquam negent Protestantes hominem in statu peccati libertatem suam habere respectu actuum divinorum & spiritualium, fatentur tamen voluntatem ejus, quantumvis peccato corruptam, actuum istorum respectu, variis modis liberam dici posse. Nec enim corruptio per peccatum inducta impedit, juxta ipsos, quominus hominis voluntas, actuum quorumvis respectu, libera sit non solum a vi externa & coactione, sed etiam a qualibet Physica necessitate, & bruta determinatione. Id solum volunt, hominis corrupti voluntatem, antequam per Dei gratiam liberetur, non esse liberam a servitute peccati, seu necessitate peccandi ex vitio. Ac proinde illam, circa bonum spirituale, carere illa libertate quae servituti opponitur.
english: Again, although the Protestants deny that man in the state of sin has his freedom with respect to divine and spiritual acts, they grant that his will, however corrupted by sin, can be called free in various ways with respect to those acts.

On their view, the corruption brought in by sin does not prevent man's will, with respect to any acts whatever, from being free not only from outside force and compulsion but also from any physical necessity and brute determination.

They hold only that the will of corrupt man, until it is set free by God's grace, is not free from bondage to sin, that is, from the necessity of sinning that comes from vice; and so, regarding spiritual good, it lacks the freedom that is opposed to bondage.

source_text: XXIV. Sic Protestantium doctrinam exponit David Paraeus. Nam proposita quaestione quam format Bellarminus, sitne homo post lapsum primi hominis vere liberi arbitrii, in iis rebus, quae pertinent ad salutem, dicit quaestionem illam lubricam & Sophisticam esse, quia, inquit, obscurum est quanam arbitrii libertatem ad divinas actiones velit, an a coactione, a Physica necessitate, a bruta determinatione: qua libertas ultro a nobis datur: an vero a servitute peccati, seu necessitate peccandi ex vitio, vel a dependentia motionis divinae: qua homini in statu peccati absque blasphemia arrogari non potest. In lib. 6. Bellar. de Grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 8.
english: David Pareus sets out the Protestant teaching this way. Taking up the question as Bellarmine frames it, 'whether man after the fall of the first man truly has free choice in the things that pertain to salvation', he calls the question slippery and sophistical.

'For,' he says, 'it is unclear what freedom of choice for divine actions he means: freedom from compulsion, from physical necessity, from brute determination, which we readily grant; or freedom from bondage to sin, that is, from the necessity of sinning that comes from vice, or from dependence on God's motion, which cannot be claimed for man in the state of sin without blasphemy.' On Bellarmine, book 6, On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 8.

source_text: XXV. Quibus consentanea sunt quae docet Josue Placeus tractatu de libero hominis arbitrio capite quarto, quod est de Libero Hominis arbitrio in statu peccati. Est, inquit, in posteris Adami facultas arbitrandi & volendi libera a triplici necessitate coactionis, scilicet, qualem pati potest corpus nostrum, determinationis a materia, maxime qualis cernitur in lapidibus & stipitibus, & sensus qualis competit brutis animantibus, cujus ratione homo est subjectum δεκτικὸν vel vitii, vel virtutis, ac Dei legi obnoxius. Quibus postea subjungit, Quam igitur arbitrii libertatem amisit Adamus? Amisit facultatem absolutam non peccandi sitam in justitia originali, quae posita est partim in naturali facultatum moralium integritate, perfectione, rectitudine absque ullo vitio, morbo, ἀταξίᾳ, errore, partim in appetitu veri finis ultimi, & ex illo appetitu enatis habitibus bene vivendi inchoatis, qui secundum naturae ordinem paulatim crevissent ad summum usque perfectionis gradum. In hujus libertatis locum successit servitus peccati sita in depravatione atque obliquitate facultatum moralium, praesertim voluntatis: ea vero depravatio consistit in aversione a vero fine ultimo, & conversione ad finem ultimum falso apparentem. Ex quo sequitur, cum quicquid appetitur sit aut finis ultimus, aut medium ad illud, nihil sani reliquum esse factum in facultatibus nostris moralibus. Neque id solum, sed quamdiu sic affecti sumus, fieri non posse quin peccemus.
english: This agrees with what Josué de la Place teaches in his treatise on man's free choice, chapter 4, which deals with man's free choice in the state of sin. 'In Adam's descendants,' he says, 'there is a faculty of judging and willing that is free from a threefold necessity: from compulsion, such as our body can suffer; from determination by matter, chiefly as seen in stones and logs; and from sense, as belongs to brute animals. Because of this faculty man is a subject capable of either vice or virtue, and answerable to God's law.'

He then adds: 'What freedom of choice, then, did Adam lose? He lost the absolute power of not sinning that lay in original righteousness. This lay partly in the natural integrity of the moral faculties, their perfection and rectitude, free of any vice, disease, disorder or error; partly in the desire for the true last end and in the habits of good living that sprang from that desire, which by the order of nature would have grown little by little to the highest degree of perfection.

In place of this freedom came the bondage of sin, which lies in the corruption and crookedness of the moral faculties, especially the will. That corruption consists in turning away from the true last end and turning toward a last end that only falsely appears to be one.

Since whatever is desired is either the last end or a means to it, it follows that nothing sound is left in our moral faculties. And more than that: as long as we are in that condition, we cannot help sinning.'

source_text: XXVI. Illud quoque hic observandum est Scholae Reformatae Doctores in hac quaestione distinguere inter potentiam proximam & activam, & inter potentiam remotam & passivam. Et concedunt hominem in statu peccati, & ante gratiam, habere quidem potentiam quandam remotam & passivam ad actus spirituales & supernaturales, sed negant hominem ita consideratum ad eosdem actus habere potentiam ullam proximam & activam. Qua distinctione utitur Paraeus in lib. 6. Bellar. de Lib. Arbitr. cap. 15.
english: A further point: on this question the Reformed doctors separate two kinds of capacity, the proximate and active kind and the remote and passive kind.

Man in the state of sin and before grace, they allow, keeps some remote, passive capacity for spiritual and supernatural acts; what they refuse him, so considered, is any proximate, active capacity for them. Pareus draws exactly this line when commenting on Bellarmine's sixth book on free choice, chapter 15.

source_text: XXVII. Et eandem etiam distinctionem adhibent Theologi Leydenses in sua purioris Theologiae Synopsi. In statu corruptionis, inquiunt, seu in homine naturaliter tantum genito, & originali peccato obstricto, quamvis is non amiserit, ut in intelligentia intellectionem, ita neque in voluntate naturalem libertatem electionis, sed retinuerit cum animae substantia naturales ejus facultates, quae actionum sunt principia, & potentiam remotam & passivam suscipiendi contrarii: attamen amisit, ut ab intelligentia, ita & a voluntate rectitudinem & bonitatem, imo contrarium habitum vitiosum accepit. Adeoque liberum arbitrium potentia proxima & activa, Diabolo instigante, sub cujus potestate & dominio est, non amplius in bonum quod vere bonum, sed tantum in malum quamvis specie bonum, attamen in generibus & gradibus mali electione remanente, necessario respectu principii proximi, sponte, voluntate, & libenter tamen fertur. Eligit enim malum, & bonum repudiat. Disputatione de Libero Arbitrio thesi 18. & 19.
english: The Leiden theologians use the same distinction in their Synopsis of Purer Theology. 'In the state of corruption,' they say, 'that is, in man begotten only by nature and bound by original sin, he has not lost the act of understanding in the intellect, nor the natural freedom of choice in the will; he has kept, with the substance of the soul, its natural faculties, which are the sources of actions, and the remote and passive power of receiving the contrary.

Yet he has lost rectitude and goodness from the intellect and likewise from the will, and has even acquired the contrary, vicious habit. So free choice, by its proximate and active power, at the prompting of the devil, under whose power and dominion it lies, no longer moves toward the good that is truly good but only toward evil, though under the appearance of good.

It still keeps a choice among the kinds and degrees of evil, and it moves necessarily as regards its proximate principle, yet spontaneously, voluntarily and willingly. For it chooses evil and rejects good.' Disputation on free choice, theses 18 and 19.
